## Evolution of Liver Transplantation (LT)
- Evolved from a high-risk procedure to a standard treatment for liver failure
- 1-year survival rates now exceed 85%
- 5-year survival rates now exceed 70%
- Despite dramatic improvements, life-threatening complications still occur
- Complications frequently result in the need for reoperation

## Shifting Demographics: The Rise of NASH
- Hepatitis C cirrhosis was historically the main indication in Europe/North America
- Effective antiviral therapies have significantly reduced HCV transplants
- Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is quickly becoming the most common indication
- Rapid increase in NASH resulting in decompensated liver failure
- Anticipated 178% increase in end-stage liver disease (ESLD) deaths by 2030

## The Obesity Epidemic and LT
- Obesity has a 2-fold effect impacting LT complications
- 1. Increasing the overall demand for donor livers
- 2. Increasing prevalence of fatty liver disease in potential organ donors
- Recipients with BMI > 30 have increased postoperative cardiopulmonary complications
- Longer intensive care unit (ICU) stays are observed in obese recipients

## Impact of Macrosteatosis in Donors
- Fatty liver disease increases discarded livers from brain-dead donors
- Increases transplanted grafts with higher degrees of macrosteatosis
- Survival rates with macrosteatosis > 30% are comparable to less fatty livers
- However, postoperative complication rates are markedly increased:
  - Postreperfusion syndrome (PRS)
  - Early allograft dysfunction (EAD)
  - Postoperative dialysis
  - Need for a second operation

## Expanding the Donor Pool
- Surgeons must operate on previously "poor" candidates
- Increased use of marginal donor livers
- Surgical techniques to increase donor pool:
  - Reduced-size grafts
  - Split-liver grafts
- These parenchymal-splitting operations introduce a new series of unique complications

## Living-Donor Liver Transplantation (LDLT) Complications
- Hepatic artery thrombosis (HAT) incidence is 2x higher in LDLT
- Bile leaks and strictures are 2x higher in LDLT
- Steep learning curve to reduce these complications
- Despite higher morbidity, patient and graft survival are similar or superior to deceased donors

## Small-for-Size Syndrome (SFSS)
- Major complication after LDLT
- Characterized by:
  - Hyperbilirubinemia
  - Coagulopathy
  - Encephalopathy shortly after transplant
- Terminology is becoming historic; Early Allograft Dysfunction (EAD) is now preferred
- Graft size is not the only factor for slow return of hepatic function

## Organ Procurement: The Process
- Begins with identification of a suitable organ
- Procurement teams dispatched for recovery
- Liver procurement team dictates dissection below the diaphragm
- Cardiac/thoracic teams work in concert for heart/lungs
- Careful planning required to minimize cold-ischemia time for heart/lungs

## Donation After Cardiac Death (DCD)
- Gained popularity since the 1990s to increase organ pool
- DCD donors increased from 6% to 11% of all US donors (2010-2019)
- Patient deemed hopeless but not "brain dead" is allowed to die naturally
- Organs procured after 2 to 5 minutes of asystole
- Concerns for increased biliary strictures and worse long-term graft survival
- Modern assessment supports comparable outcomes with appropriate donor selection

## Normothermic Perfusion Technologies
- Used to mitigate DCD complications
- Normothermic regional perfusion
- Normothermic machine perfusion
- Believed to make ischemic cholangiopathy much less common
- Improves utilization of high-risk donor grafts

## Procurement Injuries: Overview
- Occur in roughly 20% to 30% of organ donors
- Can be broken down into three categories:
  1. Parenchymal injuries
  2. Vascular injuries
  3. Bile duct injuries
- Expedited operations in unstable patients increase technical errors

## Vascular Injuries During Procurement
- Most common major injury: Aberrant hepatic artery ligation/division
- Occurs by failure to recognize replaced/accessory right or left hepatic artery
- Frequency of aberrant anatomy (Hiatt et al.):
  - Replaced/accessory right: ~10%
  - Replaced/accessory left: similar frequency
  - Dual replacement: 3%
- Hilum-replaced arteries represent 2/3 of all vascular injuries

## Consequences of Vascular Injuries
- Serious because liver segments are not perfused during recovery
- Usually require reconstruction on the back table before reimplantation
- Associated with a high rate of early HAT (30%)
- Subsequent need for re-transplantation is high

## Parenchymal and Bile Duct Injuries
- Parenchymal injuries: Most common minor injury
  - Treated with topical hemostatics, cautery, or liver stitch
  - Associated with long operative times and blood loss
  - No impact on long-term graft function
- Bile duct injuries: Less frequent
  - Caused by stripping vascular supply or cutting duct too short
  - Managed by Roux-en-Y biliary reconstruction
  - Typically not associated with graft loss

## Donor Factors: Cold Ischemia and BMI
- Prolonged cold-ischemia time contributes to recipient morbidity
- Grafts with > 12 hours cold ischemia have increased risk of graft loss
- Macrosteatosis > 30% associated with poor early graft function
- High BMI donors used less commonly
- Bedside/procurement biopsy confirms macrosteatosis, allowing safe use
- Visceral adipose tissue makes procurement technically challenging

## Perioperative Coagulopathy: The Challenge
- ESLD patients present with spectrum of coagulation abnormalities
- Combination of pro- and anti-coagulants with deranged fibrinolysis
- Prone to both massive hemorrhage and life-threatening thrombosis
- Compounded by portal hypertension and adhesions from prior surgery
- Creates a vicious cycle of worsening coagulopathy during procedure

## Assessing Coagulation: TEG and ROTEM
- Preoperative assessment guides anesthesia and surgical teams
- Blood loss incrementally increases postoperative complications
- Viscoelastic testing predicts massive transfusion:
  - Thrombelastography (TEG)
  - Rotational thrombelastography (ROTEM)
- TEG maximum amplitude outperforms INR and MELD for massive transfusion prediction
- ROTEM outperforms conventional assays for nonsurgical bleeding

## Preemptive Treatment of Coagulopathy
- Often not indicated for mild to moderate derangements
- Platelets rapidly sequestered by the spleen (historic data)
- Plasma transfusions can exacerbate venous hypertension and increase bleeding
- Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC):
  - Reduces blood loss during LT
  - Corrects INR without plasma volume
  - Associated with life-threatening thrombotic complications (use conservatively)

## The Hypercoagulable State in Cirrhosis
- Cirrhosis is an independent risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
- NASH associated with even higher risk of thrombotic complications
- Conventional coagulation measurements miss this hypercoagulable state
- Elevated preoperative TEG maximum amplitude (clot strength) = 5-fold risk of early HAT
- Intraoperative heparin bolus adopted for selected recipients with high clot strength

## Managing Portal Hypertension and TIPS
- Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) lowers portal hypertension
- May help reduce blood loss during transplantation
- Misplaced TIPS in vena cava/portal vein is life-threatening during LT
- TIPS removal is difficult and may lead to massive hemorrhage
- Temporary portocaval shunts can decompress portal circulation during hepatectomy

## Intraoperative Hemostasis and Fibrinolysis
- Native liver removal causes hyperfibrinolytic state (elevated t-PA)
- After reperfusion, majority of patients correct their fibrinolytic state
- Liver rapidly clears t-PA (half-life 5 minutes)
- Lack of t-PA clearance after reperfusion = massive bleeding
- Antifibrinolytics may be of value to improve hemostasis control

## Post-Reperfusion Fibrinolysis Shutdown
- Almost all recipients develop inhibition of fibrinolytic system 2 hours post-reperfusion
- Fibrinolysis shutdown persists beyond postoperative day 1
- Lack of capacity to break down endogenous clots
- Essential NOT to overtransfuse during this time frame
- Associated with decreased graft survival and postoperative thrombotic complications

## Postoperative Transfusion Guidelines
- Guided by clinical judgment and stable hemoglobin levels
- Target hemoglobin of 10 to promote platelet margination
- Platelet transfusion for absolute count < 30,000 or TEG MA < 50 with dropping Hgb
- Plasma transfusion for TEG R time > 10 mins or INR > 2 with dropping Hgb
- Cryoprecipitate for Clauss fibrinogen < 100 or TEG angle < 55
- > 6 hours of RBC postoperative bleeding indicates need to return to OR

## Primary Nonfunction (PNF)
- Extreme end of graft dysfunction spectrum
- Occurs in 2% to 6% of LTs
- Mortality rate up to 50% even after re-transplantation
- Major risk factors:
  - Steatosis of donor liver
  - Female/older donor
  - Long cold and warm ischemia times

## Clinical Manifestations of PNF
- Patients do not retain hepatic function; signs are not subtle
- Altered mental status
- Persistent acidosis
- Hypoglycemia
- Coagulopathy
- Hemodynamic instability
- Serum transaminases > 8000 IU/L within first 24-48 hours
- Diminished bile and urine output

## Early Allograft Dysfunction (EAD)
- Broader term capturing recipients not requiring re-transplantation
- Occurs in roughly 25% of recipients
- Associated with 7-fold increased risk of early graft loss
- 10-fold risk of mortality after transplant
- Time frame for diagnosis commonly calculated at 7 days after LT
- Olthoff et al. definition preferred for simplicity

## Risk Factors and Definitions of EAD
- Risk factors:
  - High macrosteatosis, DCD donor, recipient obesity/HCC
  - Severity of postreperfusion syndrome
  - Warm/cold ischemia time, operative time
- Model for Early Allograft Function (MEAF):
  - Continuous variable grading severity (1 to 10)
  - Based on postoperative day 3 laboratory values
  - Higher score = progressively lower graft survival

## EAD in Living-Donor Grafts
- Graft size initially a concern (Small-for-Size Syndrome)
- Pressure and flow are major contributors rather than size alone
- Graft to body weight ratio of 0.8 can be transplanted successfully
- Key prognostic factor: Portal systemic gradient < 15 mm Hg
- EAD serves as a better predictor for long-term function than small graft size

## Vascular Complications: Overview
- Major source of morbidity and graft loss
- Especially common in live-donor graft recipients
- Arterial complications account for 64% to 82% of vascular complications
- Hepatic Artery Thrombosis (HAT) is the most common arterial complication
- Overall incidence: 1.6% to 8% in adults; 15% to 26% in pediatric patients

## Hepatic Artery Thrombosis (HAT): Risk Factors
- Incidence in LDLT varies widely
- Influenced by graft type, surgeon experience, donor anatomy
- Risk factors include:
  - Donor CMV positivity in CMV-negative recipient
  - Prolonged operating time
  - Redo LT, arterial conduit, variant arterial anatomy
  - Low surgical volume

## Early vs. Late HAT
- Early HAT:
  - UNOS defines as < 7 days with AST > 3000, INR > 2.5 or acidosis
  - Qualifies for Status 1A (or MELD 40 if < 14 days)
  - Attempt revascularization; salvage is possible
- Late HAT:
  - Typically presents as biliary complication (bilomas)
  - Identified incidentally on imaging
  - Lower frequency, better prognosis, lower re-transplant rate

## Diagnosis of HAT
- Doppler ultrasound (US) is the best screening method
- Use liberally in first 2 weeks with any change in graft function
- Care must be taken to establish arterial flow within hepatic parenchyma
- Gastroduodenal artery collaterals can cause false-negative US
- Confirmation via celiac arteriography, multiphase CT, or operative exploration

## Figure 111.1: Hepatic Artery Thrombosis
- Clinical scenario: Rapid increase in serum transaminases early post-op
- Ultrasound findings: Cannot locate an intrahepatic arterial signal
- Celiac arteriography findings:
  - Shows left gastric and splenic arterial flow
  - Fails to show any contrast in the liver
- Diagnosis: Consistent with intimal dissection of the entire common hepatic artery
- Note: T-tube within the common bile duct is visible

## Figure 111.2: Hepatic Artery Reconstruction
- Principle: Immediate reconstruction with donor iliac artery allograft
- Requires early diagnosis of HAT for successful salvage
- Surgical technique shown:
  - Iliac artery graft anastomosed between the infrarenal aorta
  - Connected to the liver allograft common hepatic artery
- Ensures complete revascularization of the graft before leaving OR

## Management of HAT
- Early post-op treatment: Rapid reestablishment of arterial inflow
- Requires urgent operation with arterial reconstruction
- Uses donor iliac artery allograft or autogenous graft (saphenous vein)
- Thrombolysis/stent placement: Not common practice, limited durable success
- Intimal dissection not amenable to thrombolysis
- 50% to 70% of patients will ultimately require re-transplantation

## Portal Vein Thrombosis (PVT): Pre-Transplant
- Previously considered absolute contraindication to orthotopic LT
- Now no longer precludes successful LT but increases surgical complexity
- Found in 5% to 25% of LT recipients
- Portal vein inflow is essential for successful LT
- Pre-operative duplex or CT imaging invaluable for intraoperative planning

## Yerdel Grading System for PVT
- Grade 1: Less than 50% PVT
- Grade 2: Greater than 50% with minimal superior mesenteric vein (SMV) obstruction
- Grade 3: 100% PVT
- Grade 4: 100% PVT with SMV thrombosis
- Management:
  - Grades 1 & 2: Intraoperative thrombectomy
  - Grade 3: Jump graft
  - Grade 4: Relative contraindication unless bypass to nonmesenteric source

## Post-Transplant PVT
- Rare complication in immediate post-op period (usually technical reasons)
- Early PVT has poor prognosis (50% mortality)
- Risk factors: Post-op platelet/RBC transfusions, pre-transplant PVT
- Late PVT (months/years later): Intimal hyperplasia with cavernous transformation
- Symptoms: Ascites, splenomegaly, varices
- Treatment: Reoperation/thrombectomy (early) or angioplasty/stenting (late)

## Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Obstruction
- Rare complication (1% of patients)
- Historically: Donor IVC anastomosed to supra/infrahepatic IVC
- Piggyback technique now popular:
  - Donor suprahepatic IVC to recipient middle/left hepatic veins
  - Recipient IVC left in situ
- Benefits: Reduced blood loss, shorter warm ischemia, lower acute kidney injury

## Piggyback Technique and Outflow Obstruction
- Concerns for increased rate of outflow obstruction
- Caused by anastomotic strictures or kinking at hepatic veins
- High frequencies in LDLT and pediatric LTs
- Early high outflow obstruction confused with high CVP from volume resuscitation
- Diagnosis: Venography with segmental pressures
- Gradient > 10 mm Hg with symptoms warrants intervention (angioplasty)

## Veno-Occlusive Disease / Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome
- VOD/SOS mimics outflow obstruction
- Related to acute rejection and drug toxicity (months after transplant)
- Diagnosed via liver biopsy (fibrous obliteration of small hepatic veins)
- Most effective treatment in bone marrow patients: Defibronate
- Success in LT recipients unclear; risk of bleeding
- Alternative strategies: Steroids, increasing immunosuppression, TIPS as last line

## Biliary Complications: Overview
- Previously considered the "Achilles heel" of LT
- Improvements in operative technique have reduced complications
- Bile duct obstruction/leaks cause ~50% of technical failures
- Require reoperation in 10% to 20% of patients
- Living-donor graft recipients have 2x higher incidence than cadaveric grafts

## Biliary Leaks: Presentation and Management
- Incidence varies widely (10% to 50%)
- Most often at choledochal anastomosis or T-tube insertion site
- T-tube removal leaks occur in 25% to 40% of patients
- Symptoms: Bilious fluid in drains, pain, increased bilirubin, fever
- Diagnosis: Cholangiography, ERC, or PTC
- ERC favored for immediate endoscopic stent placement

## Biliary Strictures: Types and Causes
- Occur in 7% to 15% of patients
- Anastomotic strictures (50% of cases):
  - Early: Secondary to edema
  - Late: Compromised blood supply
- Nonanastomotic strictures (NAS):
  - Bile duct ischemia, sludge, debris
  - Associated with HAT, chronic rejection, ABO incompatibility, DCD donors

## Figure 111.3: Biliary Stricture Management
- Clinical scenario: Patient with previously created Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
- Imaging: Anastomotic stricture with dilated intrahepatic ducts
- Intervention: Percutaneous access of the Roux-en-Y limb
- Allows diagnosis and treatment with balloon dilation
- Advantage: Avoids placement of transhepatic catheters

## Figure 111.4: Nonanastomotic Stricture in DCD
- Image shows nonanastomotic biliary stricture (arrow)
- Cause: Ischemic injury to liver graft
- Donor type: Donation after cardiac death (DCD)
- Context: DCD attempts to expand donor pool but grafts are prone to ischemic injury
- Result: Bile duct strictures (ischemic cholangiopathy)

## Ischemic Cholangiopathy
- Spectrum of nonanastomotic strictures (NAS) that tends to be diffuse
- Main causes: Ischemia-reperfusion injury, immune-mediated injury, bile salt injury
- Major risk factors: HAT and DCD donors
- Clinical cholangiopathy can be rapidly progressive with necrosis
- Requires urgent re-transplantation in severe cases
- Prevention: tPA treatment in DCD donors, machine perfusion

## Renal Dysfunction and CNI Toxicity
- Observed to some degree in almost every LT patient
- Early dysfunction: Oliguria, transient creatinine increase, or acute renal failure
- Mechanism: Prerenal azotemia from intraoperative hypotension/hypovolemia
- Calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) like cyclosporine and tacrolimus are nephrotoxic
- CNI-induced renal failure occurs in ~5% of transplanted patients
- Long-term exposure is a clear risk factor for chronic renal disease

## Renal Sparing Strategies: mTOR Inhibitors
- Automatic dose reduction of CNIs years post-transplant
- Substitution with mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors
- Examples: Sirolimus (rapamycin), everolimus
- Sirolimus disadvantages: Dyslipidemia, impaired wound healing
- Impaired healing related to alterations in vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
- Associated with early HAT; wait at least 4 weeks post-LT to initiate

## Fluid and Electrolyte Disturbances
- Universal after LT due to preoperative malnutrition and ESLD
- Worsened by metabolic stress of surgery and massive fluid resuscitation
- Metabolic alkalosis: Early sign of graft function (citrate metabolism)
- Excess water/sodium: Treated with gentle diuresis (furosemide)
- Potassium: Replete carefully (tacrolimus increases serum potassium)
- Calcium, magnesium, phosphorus: Must be repleted to avoid muscle dysfunction

## Acute Cellular Rejection: Diagnosis
- Acute deterioration in allograft function with specific histologic changes
- Mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate (lymphocytes) in portal triads
- Incidence: Approximately 45%
- Early stage: Often asymptomatic (fever, abdominal pain, malaise)
- Earliest lab indicator: Elevated bilirubin, modest increase in alkaline phosphatase
- Gold standard for diagnosis: Liver histology via percutaneous biopsy

## Treatment of Acute and Chronic Rejection
- Acute Rejection Treatment (based on Banff score / RAI):
  - Mild (RAI < 4): Increase calcineurin inhibitor
  - Moderate (RAI 4-6) / Severe (RAI > 7): High-dose pulse corticosteroids
- Chronic Rejection:
  - Associated with reduced graft survival
  - Ductopenic rejection (vanishing bile duct syndrome)
  - Loss of bile ducts in > 50% of portal tracts
  - Only effective treatment: Re-transplantation

## Antibody-Mediated Rejection (AMR)
- Rare form of immunologic complication (1% of all LTs)
- Increased to 5% in patients with positive donor-specific antigen (DSA)
- Diagnosed with C4D-positive stained biopsies
- Treatment: Plasmapheresis, IVIG, B-cell depleting medication (rituximab)
- Concerns: Underdiagnosed, rising DSA may cause occult liver fibrosis

## Post-Transplant Infections: Bacterial
- Lifelong immunosuppression creates tenuous balance
- Bacterial infections tend to occur within the first month
- Risk factors: Prolonged surgery, indwelling catheters, biliary obstruction, PVT
- Common pathogens:
  - Gram-negative (E. coli, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas)
  - Gram-positive (S. aureus, coagulase-negative staph)
- Rare but significant: Listeria, Nocardia, Legionella

## Viral Infections: Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
- Most important pathogen in clinical transplantation
- Usually occurs 30 to 50 days post-transplant
- Symptoms: Fever, malaise, leukopenia, hepatitis, pneumonitis, enterocolitis
- Diagnosis: Histologically evident invasive infection or positive deep tissue culture
- Histology: Hepatocyte necrosis, "owl's eye" intranuclear inclusion
- Treatment: Reduce immunosuppression, IV ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir

## Viral Infections: HSV and EBV
- Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV):
  - Usually reactivation due to immunosuppression
  - Mild mucocutaneous disease responding to acyclovir
  - Prompt recognition prevents fulminant hepatitis
- Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV):
  - Mononucleosis-like syndrome
  - Clinical significance: Pathogenesis of Post-Transplant Lymphoproliferative Disorder (PTLD)

## Opportunistic Fungal Infections
- Clinically significant fungal infection incidence: 20% to 25%
- Invasive fungal infection (1% to 3%) has high mortality
- Risk factors: Re-transplant, high immunosuppression, Roux-en-Y, CMV, MELD > 30
- Candida: Most common, colonizes airways/biliary tract
- Aspergillus: Angioinvasive, disseminates to CNS/lungs (mortality near 100%)
- Prophylaxis (e.g., Eraxis) reduces mortality from near 100% to < 20%

## Post-Transplantation Lymphoproliferative Disorder (PTLD)
- Life-threatening complication of chronic immunosuppression
- Strongly associated with EBV replication in B cells
- Incidence: 1% to 3% among LT recipients
- Polyclonal PTLD: Treatable by discontinuing immunosuppression
- Monoclonal PTLD: Difficult to treat, high mortality
- Treatment for monoclonal: Radiation, chemotherapy, Rituximab (anti-CD20)

## Acute Immunosuppressive Drug Toxicity
- Most common agents: CNIs (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) +/- corticosteroids
- Side effects: GI disturbances, headache, tremor
- Cyclosporine: Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism
- Tacrolimus: Glucose intolerance
- Both: Hyperkalemia, nephrotoxicity (acute azotemia, chronic renal disease)
- Mycophenolate mofetil: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, increased infections

## Recurrent Hepatitis and Bone Disease
- Recurrent HBV: 80-90% recurrence in first year without prophylaxis
  - Prevented with HBIG, lamivudine, interferon
- Recurrent HCV: Universal after LT
  - Improved HCV medications offer almost 100% cure rates
- Bone Disease: Hepatic osteodystrophy common
  - Osteoporosis peaks 3-6 months post-LT
  - Atraumatic fractures, avascular necrosis from corticosteroids

## Neuropsychiatric and Metabolic Complications
- Neuropsychiatric: Anxiety, depression, seizures, encephalopathy
  - CNI toxicity causes tremors, headaches, seizures
- Hypertension: Observed in ~70% of recipients at 1 year
- Hyperlipidemia: 40% manifest metabolic syndrome
- Management: Dietary changes, exercise, statins, Omega-3 fatty acids (fish oil)
- Conclusion: Multidisciplinary team approach essential for early diagnosis and treatment
